code.title: Normalization: atomic anomalies
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# Flat table: the customer's city is repeated on every order line
db.execute("CREATE TABLE flat(order_id, customer, city, item)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO flat VALUES (?,?,?,?)",
    [(1, "Asha", "Pune", "lamp"), (2, "Asha", "Pune", "mug"), (3, "Asha", "Pune", "pen")])
# Update anomaly: Asha moves, but only one row gets changed
db.execute("UPDATE flat SET city='Delhi' WHERE order_id=1")
print("flat table cities for Asha:",
      db.execute("SELECT DISTINCT city FROM flat WHERE customer='Asha' ORDER BY 1").fetchall())
# Normalized: city lives in exactly one row
db.execute("CREATE TABLE customers(customer PRIMARY KEY, city)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE orders(order_id PRIMARY KEY, customer, item)")
db.execute("INSERT INTO customers VALUES ('Asha','Pune')")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (?,?,?)",
    [(1, "Asha", "lamp"), (2, "Asha", "mug"), (3, "Asha", "pen")])
db.execute("UPDATE customers SET city='Delhi' WHERE customer='Asha'")  # one-row update
print("normalized cities seen per order:",
      db.execute("SELECT o.order_id, c.city FROM orders o JOIN customers c USING(customer)").fetchall())
# Delete anomaly: deleting every order line loses the customer's city in the flat table
db.execute("DELETE FROM flat")
print("flat rows left (city lost):", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM flat").fetchone()[0])

followUps: In a hospital system, a visits table stores each patient's insurer phone number on every visit row. If a patient's only visit is deleted, the insurer details disappear with it, so you lose a fact you still needed. Fix: keep patients and insurers in their own tables, so deleting a visit removes only the visit.

No. Repetition is redundancy only when the repeated value is determined by something else and so could go out of sync. A foreign key repeated in many rows is not redundancy, it is how rows link. A price copied into each order line is also fine because it is a snapshot: the price at sale time is a separate fact from today's list price.

code.title: 1NF to 2NF by decomposition
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# Violates 2NF: product_name depends only on sku, part of the key (order_id, sku)
db.execute("CREATE TABLE flat(order_id, sku, qty, product_name)")
rows = [(1, "S1", 2, "Lamp"), (1, "S2", 1, "Mug"), (2, "S1", 5, "Lamp")]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO flat VALUES (?,?,?,?)", rows)
print("input:", rows)
# Check the partial dependency sku -> product_name on the data
bad = db.execute("SELECT sku FROM flat GROUP BY sku HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT product_name) > 1").fetchall()
print("sku values with 2+ names (FD broken):", bad)
# Decompose into 2NF
db.execute("CREATE TABLE products(sku PRIMARY KEY, product_name)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE order_items(order_id, sku, qty, PRIMARY KEY(order_id, sku))")
db.execute("INSERT INTO products SELECT DISTINCT sku, product_name FROM flat")
db.execute("INSERT INTO order_items SELECT order_id, sku, qty FROM flat")
print("products:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM products ORDER BY sku").fetchall())
# Rejoin and compare with EXCEPT in both directions: empty both ways means lossless
q = "SELECT order_id, sku, qty, product_name FROM order_items JOIN products USING(sku)"
print("lost rows:", db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM flat EXCEPT {q}").fetchall())
print("extra rows:", db.execute(f"{q} EXCEPT SELECT * FROM flat").fetchall())

followUps: Because 2NF only complains about a column that depends on part of a composite key, and a single-column key has no parts. In orders(order_id, date, customer), the key order_id is one column, so every other column depends on the whole key by definition. A table in 1NF with a single-column key is therefore automatically 2NF (it may still fail 3NF).

No. 3NF is defined as 2NF plus no transitive dependencies, so every 3NF table is already 2NF. The reverse is the common case: a table can be 2NF but fail 3NF, for example employees(emp_id, dept_id, dept_name) where emp_id is a single-column key but dept_name depends on dept_id. (The weaker idea of a partial dependency is simply excluded by 3NF.)

code.title: Attribute closure and candidate keys

followUps:
Attribute closure X+ is everything X determines, found by repeatedly applying FDs until nothing new is added.

  1. Start with the set X.
  2. For each FD L → R where L is inside the set, add R.
  3. Repeat until a full pass adds nothing.

Example with AB → C, C → D, D → A: {A,B} gains C, then D, so AB+ = ABCD and AB is a key. Cost: polynomial, at most n passes over the FD list.

A prime attribute is one that belongs to at least one candidate key. It matters because 3NF allows a dependency X → Y when Y is prime, while BCNF does not. In R(A,B,C,D) with keys AB, BC, BD, all four attributes are prime, so such a table is automatically 3NF, and only BCNF can still object.

code.title: BCNF split loses a dependency
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# register(student, subject, tutor): (student,subject)->tutor and tutor->subject
db.execute("CREATE TABLE register(student, subject, tutor, PRIMARY KEY(student, subject))")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO register VALUES (?,?,?)",
    [("Ann", "Math", "Rao"), ("Bob", "Math", "Rao"), ("Ann", "Art", "Lee")])
print("register:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM register").fetchall())
# Check tutor -> subject holds (it makes tutor a non-superkey determinant)
print("tutors with 2+ subjects:", db.execute(
    "SELECT tutor FROM register GROUP BY tutor HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT subject) > 1").fetchall())
# BCNF decomposition
db.execute("CREATE TABLE tutors(tutor PRIMARY KEY, subject)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE student_tutors(student, tutor, PRIMARY KEY(student, tutor))")
db.execute("INSERT INTO tutors SELECT DISTINCT tutor, subject FROM register")
db.execute("INSERT INTO student_tutors SELECT student, tutor FROM register")
# Lost dependency: Ann now has two Math tutors, and no key rejects it
db.execute("INSERT INTO tutors VALUES ('Kim', 'Math')")
db.execute("INSERT INTO student_tutors VALUES ('Ann', 'Kim')")
rows = db.execute("""SELECT st.student, t.subject, COUNT(*) FROM student_tutors st
    JOIN tutors t USING(tutor) GROUP BY st.student, t.subject HAVING COUNT(*) > 1""").fetchall()
print("violations of (student,subject)->tutor, found only via a join:", rows)

followUps:
Use a trigger, an assertion-like check, or a helper constraint so the database still enforces the rule across the two tables. A trigger on student_tutors can look up the new tutor's subject and reject the row if the student already has a different tutor for that subject:

IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM student_tutors st JOIN tutors t USING(tutor)
  WHERE st.student = NEW.student AND t.subject = (SELECT subject FROM tutors WHERE tutor = NEW.tutor))
  RAISE 'two tutors for one subject';

Alternatively keep a denormalized copy with a composite foreign key.

Usually 3NF, because it is always lossless and dependency-preserving, so keys and UNIQUE constraints enforce every rule. I would pick BCNF only when the lost dependency is unimportant or enforceable cheaply. Here the leftover anomaly in register (a tutor's subject repeated per student) is a small cost compared to silently allowing two Math tutors for one student.

code.title: Lossless vs lossy decomposition
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE emp(emp, dept, loc)")  # dept -> loc
rows = [("e1", "d1", "Pune"), ("e2", "d2", "Pune"), ("e3", "d3", "Delhi")]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO emp VALUES (?,?,?)", rows)
print("original:", rows)
# Lossless: split on dept (the common attribute dept is a key of (dept, loc))
good = "SELECT a.emp, a.dept, b.loc FROM (SELECT DISTINCT emp, dept FROM emp) a " \
       "JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT dept, loc FROM emp) b ON a.dept = b.dept"
# Lossy: split on loc (loc is not a key of either piece)
bad = "SELECT a.emp, b.dept, a.loc FROM (SELECT DISTINCT emp, loc FROM emp) a " \
      "JOIN (SELECT DISTINCT dept, loc FROM emp) b ON a.loc = b.loc"
for name, q in (("(emp,dept)+(dept,loc)", good), ("(emp,loc)+(dept,loc)", bad)):
    # EXCEPT in both directions: lost rows and spurious rows
    lost = db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM emp EXCEPT {q}").fetchall()
    extra = db.execute(f"{q} EXCEPT SELECT * FROM emp ORDER BY 1").fetchall()
    print(name, "lost:", lost, "spurious:", extra)

followUps: Projection keeps every row's values, and a natural join matches a row with its own projections. Each original row (a, b, c) produces (a, b) in R1 and (b, c) in R2, and those two match on b, so (a, b, c) is rebuilt. Joining can therefore only add extra rows (spurious), never drop one. Example: row (e1, d1, Pune) always reappears.

A lossy decomposition is the same mistake as joining on a non-unique column: each side matches many rows, so rows multiply. Joining orders to payments on order_id when an order has 2 payments repeats each order line twice and doubles SUM(amount): 30 becomes 60. The fix is the same: join on a key of at least one side, or aggregate first.

code.title: Dependency not enforceable after BCNF split
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# R(J,K,L): JK -> L and L -> K. Splitting on L -> K gives BCNF tables.
db.execute("CREATE TABLE lk(l PRIMARY KEY, k)")      # enforces L -> K by a key
db.execute("CREATE TABLE jl(j, l, PRIMARY KEY(j, l))")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO lk VALUES (?,?)", [("L1", "K1"), ("L2", "K1")])
db.execute("INSERT INTO jl VALUES ('J1', 'L1')")
# JK -> L says (J1, K1) must map to one L. Inserting J1 with L2 (also K1) breaks it,
# but both inserts are accepted: no single table holds J, K and L together.
db.execute("INSERT INTO jl VALUES ('J1', 'L2')")
print("jl:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM jl").fetchall())
print("lk:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM lk").fetchall())
# Only a join exposes the violation
rows = db.execute("""SELECT jl.j, lk.k, COUNT(DISTINCT jl.l) FROM jl JOIN lk USING(l)
    GROUP BY jl.j, lk.k HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT jl.l) > 1""").fetchall()
print("(J,K) pairs with two L values:", rows)
# Fix options: a trigger doing this join check, or keep R in 3NF with a UNIQUE(j,k) table.

followUps:
For each FD X → Y, grow X by repeatedly adding attributes from the closure computed inside the decomposition tables only. If the result contains Y, the FD is preserved. In steps:

  1. Set Z = X.
  2. For each table Ri: Z = Z ∪ ((Z ∩ Ri)+ ∩ Ri).
  3. Repeat until Z stops growing.

Never compute the full projected FD set, which is exponential. The test runs in polynomial time.

Only as a last resort. A trigger works, but it is code that must be kept in sync, can be disabled, is easy to bypass with bulk loads, and costs a join on each write. Prefer 3NF or a composite UNIQUE or foreign key. If I do accept one, I add a periodic query that searches for violations, like the HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 check on the joined tables.

code.title: Normalizing a spreadsheet with INSERT SELECT DISTINCT
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE sheet(order_id, date, customer, city, sku, name, price, qty)")
rows = [(1, "2026-01-02", "Asha", "Pune", "S1", "Lamp", 20, 1),
        (1, "2026-01-02", "Asha", "Pune", "S2", "Mug", 5, 2),
        (2, "2026-01-03", "Ravi", "Delhi", "S1", "Lamp", 20, 3)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO sheet VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?,?,?)", rows)
print("sheet rows:", len(rows))
# The primary keys reject any row that contradicts a functional dependency
db.execute("CREATE TABLE customers(customer PRIMARY KEY, city)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE products(sku PRIMARY KEY, name)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE orders(order_id PRIMARY KEY, date, customer)")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE order_items(order_id, sku, qty, price_at_sale, PRIMARY KEY(order_id, sku))")
db.execute("INSERT INTO customers SELECT DISTINCT customer, city FROM sheet")
db.execute("INSERT INTO products SELECT DISTINCT sku, name FROM sheet")
db.execute("INSERT INTO orders SELECT DISTINCT order_id, date, customer FROM sheet")
db.execute("INSERT INTO order_items SELECT order_id, sku, qty, price FROM sheet")
# Rejoin and compare in both directions
q = """SELECT o.order_id, o.date, o.customer, c.city, i.sku, p.name, i.price_at_sale, i.qty
       FROM order_items i JOIN orders o USING(order_id)
       JOIN customers c USING(customer) JOIN products p USING(sku)"""
print("missing:", db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM sheet EXCEPT {q}").fetchall())
print("extra:", db.execute(f"{q} EXCEPT SELECT * FROM sheet").fetchall())

followUps:
The PK on the new products table rejects the second name, and the INSERT fails. That is useful: it proves the FD sku → name is false in your data, so you must resolve the conflict before migrating. Find the cause first:

SELECT sku, COUNT(DISTINCT name) FROM sheet
GROUP BY sku HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT name) > 1;

Typos need cleanup; real renames need history (SCD2).

Use expand and contract. 1) Create the new tables and add the new columns alongside the old ones. 2) Backfill in small batches, then keep both in sync with dual writes or triggers. 3) Switch reads to the new tables behind a flag and compare results. 4) Stop writing the old columns, then drop them in a later release. Every step is backward compatible, so you can roll back at any point.

code.title: Denormalized counter with trigger and drift check
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE posts(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, title, like_count INTEGER DEFAULT 0);
CREATE TABLE likes(post_id, user, PRIMARY KEY(post_id, user));
-- Denormalized counter kept in sync by triggers, in the same transaction as the write
CREATE TRIGGER like_add AFTER INSERT ON likes
  BEGIN UPDATE posts SET like_count = like_count + 1 WHERE id = NEW.post_id; END;
CREATE TRIGGER like_del AFTER DELETE ON likes
  BEGIN UPDATE posts SET like_count = like_count - 1 WHERE id = OLD.post_id; END;
INSERT INTO posts(id, title) VALUES (1, 'Hello'), (2, 'World');
INSERT INTO likes VALUES (1,'a'), (1,'b'), (1,'c'), (2,'a');
""")
print("counters:", db.execute("SELECT id, like_count FROM posts").fetchall())
db.execute("DELETE FROM likes WHERE post_id=1 AND user='c'")
print("after unlike:", db.execute("SELECT id, like_count FROM posts").fetchall())
# Simulate drift (a bug or a manual edit), then detect it with a reconcile query
db.execute("UPDATE posts SET like_count = 99 WHERE id = 2")
drift = db.execute("""SELECT p.id, p.like_count, COUNT(l.user) FROM posts p
    LEFT JOIN likes l ON l.post_id = p.id GROUP BY p.id
    HAVING p.like_count != COUNT(l.user)""").fetchall()
print("drifted (id, stored, real):", drift)

followUps: The most reliable way is to make the copy a derived value that is updated in the same transaction as its source, or rebuilt from the source. For counters use a trigger or a transactional UPDATE; for cross-service copies use an outbox table plus consumers that apply events idempotently. Run a reconcile query (compare stored value to real COUNT) on a schedule and alert on any drift; accept a documented lag when updates are asynchronous.

The copy drifts, and the last writer wins with no one knowing which was right. Example: service A sets city = Pune while service B sets Delhi, and the order of messages decides. Avoid it by giving each fact one owner service: only the owner writes, others read or subscribe to its change events, and a reconcile job flags disagreement.

code.title: Star schema query and fan-out at the wrong grain
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.executescript("""
-- Dimensions are denormalized: category is stored right inside dim_product
CREATE TABLE dim_product(product_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name, category);
CREATE TABLE dim_date(date_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, month);
-- Grain: ONE ROW PER ORDER LINE
CREATE TABLE fact_sales(order_id, line_no, product_id, date_id, amount, PRIMARY KEY(order_id, line_no));
INSERT INTO dim_product VALUES (1,'Lamp','Home'), (2,'Mug','Home'), (3,'Pen','Office');
INSERT INTO dim_date VALUES (20260101,'2026-01'), (20260201,'2026-02');
INSERT INTO fact_sales VALUES (1,1,1,20260101,20), (1,2,2,20260101,10),
  (2,1,3,20260201,5), (3,1,1,20260201,20);
""")
# A star query: one join per dimension, then group by dimension attributes
rows = db.execute("""SELECT d.month, p.category, SUM(f.amount)
    FROM fact_sales f JOIN dim_product p USING(product_id) JOIN dim_date d USING(date_id)
    GROUP BY d.month, p.category ORDER BY 1, 2""").fetchall()
for r in rows:
    print(r)
# Wrong grain example: joining a table with several rows per order double counts amounts
db.execute("CREATE TABLE payments(order_id, part)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO payments VALUES (?,?)", [(1, "card"), (1, "voucher")])
print("true total for order 1:", db.execute("SELECT SUM(amount) FROM fact_sales WHERE order_id=1").fetchone()[0])
print("fan-out total:", db.execute(
    "SELECT SUM(amount) FROM fact_sales f JOIN payments p USING(order_id) WHERE order_id=1").fetchone()[0])

followUps: A degenerate dimension is an identifier that lives in the fact table with no dimension table of its own, because it has no attributes to describe. Example: order_number or invoice_id on an order-line fact. It is used to group lines of the same order and to trace back to the source system, so you keep it as a plain column.

Type 1 overwrites the old value: when a customer moves from Pune to Delhi, past facts now show Delhi, so history is lost but queries stay simple. Type 2 adds a new row with valid_from, valid_to and a new surrogate key, so old facts still point to the Pune row. Example: 100 orders in Pune stay under Pune and new ones go to Delhi. Type 2 costs more rows and joins.

code.title: Comma list vs child table
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# Version A: comma list in one column (violates 1NF)
db.execute("CREATE TABLE post_a(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, tags)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO post_a VALUES (?,?)", [(1, "java,sql"), (2, "javascript"), (3, "c,cpp")])
print("A: LIKE '%java%' ->", db.execute("SELECT id FROM post_a WHERE tags LIKE '%java%'").fetchall(),
      "(post 2 is a false match)")
# Version B: child table, one row per tag
db.execute("CREATE TABLE post_tags(post_id, tag, PRIMARY KEY(post_id, tag))")
for pid, tags in [(1, "java,sql"), (2, "javascript"), (3, "c,cpp")]:
    for t in tags.split(","):
        db.execute("INSERT INTO post_tags VALUES (?,?)", (pid, t))
print("B: tag = 'java' ->", db.execute("SELECT post_id FROM post_tags WHERE tag='java'").fetchall())
# Per-element facts are easy: count posts per tag, enforce uniqueness via the key
print("B: posts per tag:", db.execute("SELECT tag, COUNT(*) FROM post_tags GROUP BY tag ORDER BY tag").fetchall())
try:
    db.execute("INSERT INTO post_tags VALUES (1, 'java')")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("B: duplicate tag rejected:", e)

followUps:
Create the child table, copy the elements, verify, then drop the column. Steps:

  1. CREATE TABLE post_tags(post_id, tag, PRIMARY KEY(post_id, tag)).
  2. Expand with jsonb_array_elements_text(tags) (PostgreSQL) in an INSERT … SELECT.
  3. Compare counts and run EXCEPT both ways.
  4. Switch readers, then drop the old column.
INSERT INTO post_tags
SELECT id, jsonb_array_elements_text(tags) FROM posts;

PostgreSQL offers a GIN index on a jsonb column, which speeds containment (@>) and key-existence (?) queries over the whole document. The jsonb_path_ops operator class is smaller and faster for @> only. For one frequently filtered key, an ordinary B-tree expression index such as ((data->>'status')) is usually better. A GIN index adds write cost, so index only the queries you run.

code.title: 4NF removes a cross product
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# Course has teachers and textbooks that are independent of each other (MVDs)
db.execute("CREATE TABLE ctb(course, teacher, book, PRIMARY KEY(course, teacher, book))")
for t in ("Rao", "Lee"):
    for b in ("B1", "B2"):
        db.execute("INSERT INTO ctb VALUES ('Math', ?, ?)", (t, b))
print("one table rows:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ctb").fetchone()[0], "(2 teachers x 2 books)")
# Adding a third book forces a row for EVERY teacher
for t in ("Rao", "Lee"):
    db.execute("INSERT INTO ctb VALUES ('Math', ?, 'B3')", (t,))
print("after adding B3:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ctb").fetchone()[0], "rows")
# 4NF: one table per independent fact
db.execute("CREATE TABLE ct AS SELECT DISTINCT course, teacher FROM ctb")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE cb AS SELECT DISTINCT course, book FROM ctb")
print("split rows:", db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM ct").fetchone()[0], "+",
      db.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM cb").fetchone()[0])
q = "SELECT course, teacher, book FROM ct JOIN cb USING(course)"
print("lossless:", db.execute(f"SELECT * FROM ctb EXCEPT {q}").fetchall() == [] and
      db.execute(f"{q} EXCEPT SELECT * FROM ctb").fetchall() == [])

followUps: Yes. In a BCNF relation every non-trivial FD has a superkey on the left, and 4NF only adds a rule about multivalued dependencies on top of BCNF. So 4NF implies BCNF, but a BCNF table can still fail 4NF: course(teacher, book) with independent teachers and books has no FDs at all, so it is in BCNF, yet it still holds a forced cross product.

You cannot prove an MVD from data, only look for signs and confirm with the business rule. Sign: for each course, the set of (teacher, book) pairs equals the full cross product of its teachers and its books. Test it:

SELECT course FROM t GROUP BY course
HAVING COUNT(*) = COUNT(DISTINCT teacher) * COUNT(DISTINCT book);

Courses returned fit the pattern. Example: 2 teachers, 3 books gives 6 rows.

code.title: Surrogate key still needs a UNIQUE natural key
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
# Surrogate id as PK, but no UNIQUE on the natural key: duplicates sneak in
db.execute("CREATE TABLE items_bad(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id, sku, qty)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO items_bad(order_id, sku, qty) VALUES (?,?,?)",
               [(1, "S1", 2), (1, "S1", 2)])
print("without UNIQUE:", db.execute("SELECT * FROM items_bad").fetchall())
# Keep the natural candidate key declared UNIQUE
db.execute("CREATE TABLE items(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id, sku, qty, UNIQUE(order_id, sku))")
db.execute("INSERT INTO items(order_id, sku, qty) VALUES (1, 'S1', 2)")
try:
    db.execute("INSERT INTO items(order_id, sku, qty) VALUES (1, 'S1', 2)")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError as e:
    print("with UNIQUE, rejected:", e)
# The partial dependency sku -> name still exists, so still split it out
db.execute("CREATE TABLE flat(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, order_id, sku, name)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO flat(order_id, sku, name) VALUES (?,?,?)",
               [(1, "S1", "Lamp"), (2, "S1", "Lamp")])
print("name repeated per sku:", db.execute("SELECT sku, COUNT(*), COUNT(DISTINCT name) FROM flat GROUP BY sku").fetchall())

followUps: UUIDv4 is random, which fragments B-tree indexes and causes page splits on inserts; it is 16 bytes. UUIDv7 starts with a timestamp, so it is roughly sorted like a bigint but still unique across systems. A bigint identity is smallest (8 bytes) and fastest but guessable and hard to generate across shards. My default: bigint for a single database, UUIDv7 for distributed or public IDs, UUIDv4 only when ordering leaks must be avoided.

Use a natural key when it is truly stable, unique and meaningful, and when it is small: country code (IN), currency code (USD), or a lookup table's short code. These make rows readable and joins self-explaining. Avoid natural keys that change (email, phone, name) or are long, because every foreign key copies them. If unsure, use a surrogate plus a UNIQUE natural key.

code.title: Verify proposed FDs on data
code.python:
import sqlite3
db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE wide(order_id, customer, city, sku, product, price)")
rows = [(1, "Asha", "Pune", "S1", "Lamp", 20), (2, "Asha", "Pune", "S2", "Mug", 5),
        (3, "Ravi", "Delhi", "S1", "Lamp", 20), (4, "Ravi", "Delhi", "S1", "Lampshade", 20),
        (5, "Asha", "Mumbai", "S3", "Pen", 2)]
db.executemany("INSERT INTO wide VALUES (?,?,?,?,?,?)", rows)
print("rows loaded:", len(rows))
# Verify each proposed FD on the full data: a determinant with 2+ right values breaks it
fds = [("customer", "city"), ("sku", "product"), ("sku", "price"), ("order_id", "customer")]
for x, y in fds:
    bad = db.execute(f"SELECT {x}, COUNT(DISTINCT {y}) FROM wide GROUP BY {x} "
                     f"HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT {y}) > 1").fetchall()
    # Data can only disprove an FD; no violations means "holds so far"
    print(f"{x} -> {y}:", "violated by " + str(bad) if bad else "holds on this data")

followUps: The usual ones: treating one sample as proof of a dependency (a city that is the same in 5 rows is not city → zip), splitting every column into its own table, normalizing snapshot columns like price_at_sale or ship-to address that must stay frozen, forgetting UNIQUE on natural keys, and picking a surrogate key without declaring the real key. Also ignoring nulls and dirty data such as 'Pune ' and 'pune'. I treat the output as a draft.

Run it on a copy with production-sized data and do a dry run first. Check that every constraint (PK, FK, UNIQUE) loads without rejection, compare row counts and per-table checksums, and run EXCEPT both ways between the old wide table and the rejoined result. Replay your top 20 real queries on both and compare results and plans, then rehearse the rollback. Only then schedule the cut-over.

code.title: OLTP to warehouse with reconciliation
code.python:
import sqlite3
oltp = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")   # source of truth, normalized
wh = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")     # warehouse, denormalized
oltp.executescript("""
CREATE TABLE customers(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name, city);
CREATE TABLE orders(id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, customer_id, total);
INSERT INTO customers VALUES (1,'Asha','Pune'), (2,'Ravi','Delhi');
INSERT INTO orders VALUES (10,1,30), (11,1,20), (12,2,50);
""")
wh.execute("CREATE TABLE fact_orders(order_id, customer_name, city, total)")
def load():
    # Batch ELT step: join in OLTP and rebuild the wide fact (a stand-in for CDC + dbt)
    rows = oltp.execute("""SELECT o.id, c.name, c.city, o.total
        FROM orders o JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id""").fetchall()
    wh.execute("DELETE FROM fact_orders")
    wh.executemany("INSERT INTO fact_orders VALUES (?,?,?,?)", rows)
load()
print("warehouse:", wh.execute("SELECT * FROM fact_orders ORDER BY 1").fetchall())
oltp.execute("INSERT INTO orders VALUES (13, 2, 40)")  # new order, warehouse lags
# Reconciliation: compare totals; a mismatch means lag or a bug
a = oltp.execute("SELECT SUM(total) FROM orders").fetchone()[0]
b = wh.execute("SELECT SUM(total) FROM fact_orders").fetchone()[0]
print("oltp total", a, "warehouse total", b, "->", "OK" if a == b else "DRIFT")
load()
b = wh.execute("SELECT SUM(total) FROM fact_orders").fetchone()[0]
print("after refresh:", a, b, "->", "OK" if a == b else "DRIFT")

followUps: A hard delete in the source leaves no row to read, so CDC must capture it from the log as a delete event. Choose a strategy: apply it as a real delete in the warehouse, or write a tombstone or soft-delete flag (is_deleted, deleted_at) so history stays and reports can exclude it. With batch ELT that only selects new rows, deletes are missed unless you compare keys or use full snapshots. Reconcile row counts to catch missed deletes.

A conformed dimension is one dimension table shared by several fact tables with the same keys and meaning, such as dim_date or dim_customer used by both sales and returns facts. It lets you compare or join results across facts (sales per customer minus returns per customer) because everyone agrees on what a customer or a month is.
